title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution processed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) using 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic accounting that demonstrates single shared initial generation per task, the randomized 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the execution bundle described below.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps productivity but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair is conditional on three factors: (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy; (ii) validator coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and a sealed execution plan: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The experiment uses a paired shared‑initial design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if needed, issuing a single automated repair on that same candidate.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies show that large language models make factual errors and hallucinations and that detection/mitigation strategies (retrieval/RAG, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained agent architectures) can reduce but not eliminate errors. Prior NetOps prototypes demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation yet commonly lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations or preregistered causal contrasts between generator‑only and validator‑assisted pipelines. Red‑team and agent‑audit studies document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection that can alter safety outcomes. Architectural proposals therefore recommend verifier integration (deterministic validators or emulators) and bounded‑autonomy guardrails. Our study contributes a preregistered, artifact‑archived, paired measurement that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic validator+repair on identical generator outputs, addressing a specific operational evaluation gap in the literature.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistered study (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and a target 50% relative reduction; those assumptions were used only to justify sample size and are documented in the preregistration.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration task bank with 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states plus workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima). The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces syntax and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector and was applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches.

Shared‑initial adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system performed a single model invocation and reused the same initial candidate for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. Determinism in this run therefore results from adapter enforced reuse of a single model response per task, not from asserting a particular numeric temperature via the provider. The archived model configuration records "requested_model": "gpt-5-mini" and does not include an explicit numeric temperature override for the provider (the adapter did not expose a temperature field to the provider call). Deterministic accounting artifacts demonstrate single shared initial invocations per task: hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts indicate shared_initial_generation = 200; pair accounting and episode counts are consistent (complete_pair_count = 200). These archived artifacts establish that the paired contrast removed sampling variance by design; this is a preplanned trade‑off to isolate the marginal effect of performing validation and (if needed) repair on the same generator output.

Repair policy, budgeting, and analysis plan. If the primary validator reported violations, the adapter would issue at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM and revalidate the repaired candidate. The primary confirmatory test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table (n11, n10, n01, n00). Secondary/exploratory analyses (preplanned) include descriptive repair‑iteration statistics, GVR‑introduced failure rates, and exploratory regressions; these are executed only if repair events occur. All design choices, stopping rules, seeds, and handling rules were frozen before any model calls and are archived with the execution bundle.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run executed under the frozen plan and completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), repair_calls_used = 0, maximum_model_calls permitted = 400. Adapter/provider audit fields record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 200, confirming that the adapter enforced single shared invocations per task.

Primary outcomes and paired contingency. Every initial candidate passed the deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed paired difference = 0.0. The preplanned exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because there are no discordant pairs, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be evaluated in this sample: the baseline validator‑detected failure rate is 0%.

Replicated emulator holdout and contamination check. The preregistered Mininet secondary check executed on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) and the contamination summary reports zero validator–emulator disagreement flags for that holdout. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw that 10% Mininet holdout is not labeled in the archived artifact set, which prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of which tasks comprised the holdout even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements.

Representative diagnostics and empty secondary statistics. Representative per‑task validator traces confirm validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true with violation_count = 0. Difficulty labels in traces include "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" and patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change, and rolling_access_vlan_migration, demonstrating the benchmark exercised nontrivial workflow constraints. No repair attempts occurred; consequently, secondary estimands about repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failures, and model‑call cost per successful repair are empty for this run and are recorded as such in the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate paired result (n11 = 200, no discordant pairs) is an artifact‑grounded observation: under the frozen generator/prompt policy and shared‑initial adapter semantics every produced candidate satisfied the primary deterministic validator. This outcome is not evidence that repair is universally unnecessary; rather it shows that GVR provides no marginal validator‑detected benefit on this workload under the specific generation policy and validator coverage.

Why the null occurred. Archived validator traces show matched parsed_command_count and required_command_count per task, indicating generated sequences satisfied machine‑checkable constraints. The adapter accounting shows single shared model invocations per task; by design this suppressed sampling variance that might otherwise have produced failing draws that repair could fix. The Mininet holdout found no validator–emulator disagreements in its 20‑task sample, but holdout selection reproducibility is limited by the missing labeled seed.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational implications. The paired shared‑initial design isolates the incremental effect of validating and repairing a fixed candidate but cannot measure unconditional failure prevalence or the potential benefit of multi‑sample generation strategies. Practitioners should therefore (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence under their intended generation policy, (2) expand validator fidelity and emulation checks to reveal blind spots, and (3) consider multi‑sample or ensemble generation plus larger repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial. When baseline validator failures are rare, single‑pass repair budgets deliver limited marginal benefit for validator‑detectable errors; resources may be better allocated to validator improvement and adversarial testing.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration and deterministic adapter enforcement (audit fields confirm accounting). Construct validity depends on validator expressiveness: deterministic validators codify a finite set of checks and may miss device idiosyncrasies only observable in richer testbeds. External validity is limited by a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), the shared‑initial deterministic sampling policy, and the curated synthetic/public task bank. Conclusion validity: with zero discordant observations the primary confirmatory test is uninformative about the preregistered effect size, but the observed counts and exact test results are artifact‑grounded and reproducible within the archived bundle aside from the Mininet‑holdout seed gap noted above.

Recommended next steps. Future confirmatory work should (i) include independent per‑condition multi‑sample draws to estimate unconditional failure prevalence; (ii) increase or vary the repair budget (multi‑step repairs and human escalation); (iii) expand emulator/real device holdouts and explicitly record holdout selection seeds; and (iv) evaluate additional models or ensembles to probe model‑dependent brittleness. The archived artifacts provide a reproducible template for these extensions.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding a paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, automated repair yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity with richer emulation or real‑device checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution artifacts and analysis outputs are archived and available for audit in the execution bundle referenced below.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
